name: Zitkala-Ša
tagline: The pen that fought an empire
story:
In 1901, Zitkala-Ša — born Gertrude Simmons on the Yankton Reservation — did something no Native American woman had done before. She published a series of autobiographical essays in the Atlantic Monthly, laying bare the brutal reality of the Indian boarding school system that had tried to erase her identity. She was 25, alone in a literary world that saw her people as relics, and she wrote anyway.

As a child, missionaries had lured her from her mother's home with promises of red apples and education. What she found was a prison of forced assimilation — her braids cut off, her Lakota language forbidden, her spirit bent but never broken. Years later, armed with a violin and a voice that could fill concert halls, she chose the weapon that would wound deepest: the truth, written in her colonizers' own language.

For the next four decades, Zitkala-Ša fought on every front. She composed an opera — the first by a Native American woman. She co-authored a damning exposé of government corruption on Oklahoma oil lands that robbed tribes of millions. She founded the National Council of American Indians and lobbied relentlessly until the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 finally recognized her people as citizens of their own homeland.

She never recovered her Lakota name in the eyes of the law, so she gave herself one: Zitkala-Ša, 'Red Bird.' A creature that sings even in winter. She died in 1938, decades before the world caught up to what she'd been saying all along — that erasure is not education, and silence is not peace.
